content.title: Extracting the Five-Number Summary from Frequency Tables
content.overview: This lesson teaches how to derive the five-number summary—Minimum, First Quartile (Q1), Median, Third Quartile (Q3), and Maximum—from data presented in frequency tables or histograms. These five values are the essential components used to construct and interpret boxplots.
learning_objectives: Calculate the total number of data points (n) from a frequency table.
Construct a cumulative frequency column to locate specific data positions.
Apply the median-splitting rule to identify Q1, Median, and Q3 for both even and odd datasets.
Identify the Minimum and Maximum values from a frequency distribution.

sections.title: The Five-Number Summary and Boxplots
sections.content: The five-number summary provides a snapshot of a dataset's distribution. The Minimum is the smallest value with a non-zero frequency. The Maximum is the largest value with a non-zero frequency. The Median (Q2) is the middle value of the sorted data. The First Quartile (Q1) is the median of the lower half of the data, and the Third Quartile (Q3) is the median of the upper half. On a boxplot, these five values mark the left whisker end, the left edge of the box, the internal line, the right edge of the box, and the right whisker end, respectively.

sections.title: Cumulative Counts: Finding Positions
sections.content:
When data is in a frequency table, do not list every number manually. Instead, calculate the total number of observations (n) by summing the frequencies. Then, create a 'cumulative count' column by adding each frequency to the sum of all previous frequencies. This column tells you the range of positions (indices) each value occupies. For example, if the first value has a frequency of 3, it occupies positions 1, 2, and 3. If the next value has a frequency of 2, it occupies positions 4 and 5.

![A flowchart showing the steps: Sum Frequencies, Create Cumulative Counts, Find Median, Split Data, Find Q1 and Q3.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/b2d571a1-8edb-4ee8-8fe5-245646c7b02a-1786506133590-234.webp)

sections.title: The Median-Splitting Rule
sections.content: To find the quartiles, first find the Median. If n is even, the median is the average of the two middle numbers (at positions n/2 and n/2 + 1). The data is split into two equal halves of n/2 elements. Q1 is the median of the lower half, and Q3 is the median of the upper half. If n is odd, the median is the single middle number at position (n+1)/2. When finding Q1 and Q3 for an odd n, exclude the median itself and find the medians of the remaining lower and upper halves.

worked_examples.question: A survey recorded the number of pets per household: 0 pets (freq: 2), 1 pet (freq: 5), 2 pets (freq: 4), 3 pets (freq: 3), 4 pets (freq: 1). Find the five-number summary.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Find n. n = 2 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 15. Step 2: Create cumulative counts. 0 pets: pos 1-2; 1 pet: pos 3-7; 2 pets: pos 8-11; 3 pets: pos 12-14; 4 pets: pos 15. Step 3: Find Min and Max. Min = 0, Max = 4. Step 4: Find Median. Since n=15 (odd), the median is at position (15+1)/2 = 8. Position 8 corresponds to '2 pets'. Median = 2. Step 5: Find Q1 and Q3. Exclude the median (pos 8). The lower half is positions 1-7. The median of 7 items is the 4th item. Position 4 is '1 pet'. Q1 = 1. The upper half is positions 9-15. The median of these 7 items is the 4th item in that set (position 12). Position 12 is '3 pets'. Q3 = 3. Summary: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

common_mistakes: Confusing frequency with the data value itself (e.g., saying the median is the middle frequency number rather than the value associated with the middle position).
Forgetting to average the two middle values when n is even.
Including the median in the quartile calculations when n is odd, which leads to incorrect Q1 and Q3 values.
exam_tips: Always check that Min ≤ Q1 ≤ Median ≤ Q3 ≤ Max. If your Q1 is higher than your Median, you have made a calculation error.
On the ACT, if n is large, use the cumulative count to quickly jump to the required index rather than writing out a long list of numbers.
The 'box' in a boxplot represents the Interquartile Range (IQR), which is Q3 minus Q1.
content.recap: To find a five-number summary from a frequency table, sum the frequencies to find n, use cumulative counts to locate the positions of the median and quartiles, and identify the lowest and highest values with non-zero frequencies.

knowledge_claims.content: The five-number summary consists of the Minimum, First Quartile (Q1), Median, Third Quartile (Q3), and Maximum.
To find the total number of observations (n) in a frequency table, sum all values in the frequency column.
Cumulative counts are calculated by adding each category's frequency to the sum of all preceding frequencies to determine the rank-order positions of data values.
The Minimum is the smallest data value in a table that has a frequency greater than zero.
The Maximum is the largest data value in a table that has a frequency greater than zero.
If the total number of observations (n) is even, the median is the arithmetic average of the values at positions n/2 and (n/2) + 1.
If the total number of observations (n) is odd, the median is the single value located at position (n + 1) / 2.
When n is even, the dataset is split into two equal halves of n/2 elements to calculate Q1 and Q3.
When n is odd, the median value is excluded from the dataset before splitting the remaining values into lower and upper halves to calculate Q1 and Q3.
Q1 is defined as the median of the lower half of a sorted dataset.
Q3 is defined as the median of the upper half of a sorted dataset.
A valid five-number summary must satisfy the inequality condition: Minimum ≤ Q1 ≤ Median ≤ Q3 ≤ Maximum.
In a boxplot visualization, the vertical line inside the box represents the Median, while the edges of the box represent Q1 and Q3.
A common error is identifying the median as the middle value in the frequency column rather than the data value associated with the middle position of n.
